## Vocabulary

- [Fixed image - the image that doesn't move]{.fragment fragment-index=1}
- [Moving image - the image that is being aligned]{.fragment fragment-index=2}

## What is registration?

Registration is the process of aligning two or more images. 

To setup a registration problem, we need to define:

::: {.incremental}
1. **What are we matching?** — interest points, or pixels
2. **How is the image allowed to move?** — defining the transformation type
3. **How do we score a match?** — a numerical way of representing how well the images are aligned
:::

# Types of registration
Points vs pixels

## Point-based (landmark) registration {.smaller}

::: {.incremental}
- Uses a sparse set of corresponding landmarks
  - Fiducial markers
  - Anatomical landmarks
  - Detected features (e.g. nuclei centroids)
:::

::: {.fragment}
![](img/registration_point_based.png){.nostretch .absolute width="90%"}
:::

## Pixel-based (intensity) {.smaller}

::: {.incremental}
- Uses the full grid of intensity values
- No manual point-picking
- Uses the available texture
:::

![](img/registration_pixel_based.png){.fragment .nostretch .absolute top="42%" left="4%" width="92%"}


# Transformation Types
How is the image allowed to move?

## Linear vs Non-linear transforms {.smaller}

::: {.fragment}
- Linear transforms — the whole image moves as a single rigid sheet
  - Parameterized by a small number of degrees of freedom
  - Translation, rotation, scaling, shear
:::
::: {.fragment}
- Non-linear transforms — different parts of the image can move independently
  - Parameterized by a large number of degrees of freedom
  - Can capture local tissue stretching, tearing, and compression
:::

## Linear: rigid {.smaller}

::: {.incremental}
- Translation + rotation only
- Distances and angles preserved; nothing stretches
:::

![](img/registration_flexibility_rigid.png){.fragment .nostretch .absolute bottom="20%" right="2.5%" width="100%"}

## Linear: similarity {.smaller}

::: {.incremental}
- Rigid and one uniform scale factor
- Same zoom in all directions
:::

![](img/registration_flexibility_similarity.png){.fragment .nostretch .absolute bottom="20%" right="2.5%" width="100%"}

## Linear: affine {.smaller}

::: {.incremental}
- Adds shear and independent per-axis scaling
- Parallel lines stay parallel, but shapes can skew and stretch unevenly
:::

![](img/registration_flexibility_affine.png){.fragment .nostretch .absolute bottom="20%" right="2.5%" width="100%"}

## Linear vs Non-linear transforms {.smaller}

Reminder:

- Linear transforms — the whole image moves as a single rigid sheet
  - Parameterized by a small number of degrees of freedom
  - Translation, rotation, scaling, shear
- Non-linear transforms — different parts of the image can move independently
  - Parameterized by a large number of degrees of freedom
  - Can capture local tissue stretching, tearing, and compression

## Non-linear {.smaller}

![](img/registration_flexibility_nonlinear.png){.nostretch .absolute bottom="20%" right="2.5%" width="100%"}

## Non-linear: types {.smaller}


::: {.fragment}
- Thin-plate spline (TPS)
  - Given landmark pairs, finds the smoothest deformation
  - Interpolates smoothly in between the points
:::
::: {.fragment}
- B-spline
  - A coarse grid of control points where each deforms the nearby region
  - Grid spacing controls flexibility
:::
::: {.fragment}
- Diffeomorphic (ANTs SyN)
  - Image can bend and stretch, but cannot tear, fold over itself, or collapse to a point
:::

## TPS vs B-spline {.smaller}

![](img/registration_nonlinear_compared.png){.nostretch .absolute bottom="2.5%" right="2.5%" height="80%"}

## Discussion {.smaller}

Manual serial sections from one tissue block are often torn or locally stretched by
different amounts in different regions during processing.

You have a handful of usable landmarks — maybe 8.

Rigid, affine, piecewise affine, or fully non-linear?


# Similarity Metrics
How can we tell images are aligned?

## Similarity metrics {.smaller}

::: {.incremental}
- A numerical score of how well two images or sets of points match
- We will write every one of them so that **higher is better**
- Once you have a similarity metric, optimisation is possible!
:::

::: {.fragment .smaller}
You will also see these called *loss*, *cost*, or *objective* functions — those
count errors, so they run the other way up. Same information, opposite sign.
:::

## Negative mean squared error {.smaller}

::: {.incremental}
- Mean squared error (MSE)
  - Mean of the squared differences between corresponding pixels
- That sum counts *error*, so we flip its sign and use **-MSE**
  - A perfect match scores 0 — the best you can do; anything worse is negative
- Best used when the two images are directly comparable
  - Same stain, same modality, same exposure, same contrast
:::

![](img/registration_inputs_MSE_sweep.png){.nostretch .fragment .absolute bottom="2%" right="20%" width="60%"}
![](img/registration_loss_MSE_sweep.gif){.nostretch .fragment .absolute bottom="2%" right="20%" width="60%"}

## Negative mean squared error {.smaller}

![](img/registration_inputs_MSE_contrast.png){.nostretch .absolute bottom="10%" right="12.5%" width="75%"}
![](img/registration_loss_MSE_contrast.png){.nostretch .fragment .absolute bottom="10%" right="12.5%" width="75%"}

## Cross-correlation {.smaller}

::: {.incremental}
- Measures how well the two images co-vary — do changes in intensity correlate between the two images?
- A perfect match has a correlation of 1; smaller numbers are worse
- More forgiving than -MSE about overall brightness
:::

![](img/registration_inputs_correlation_sweep.png){.nostretch .fragment .absolute bottom="2.5%" right="12.5%" width="75%"}
![](img/registration_loss_correlation_sweep.gif){.nostretch .fragment .absolute bottom="2.5%" right="12.5%" width="75%"}

## Cross-correlation {.smaller}

![](img/registration_inputs_correlation.png){.nostretch .absolute top="20%" right="2.5%" width="95%"}
![](img/registration_loss_correlation.png){.nostretch .fragment .absolute top="20%" right="2.5%" width="95%"}

## Mutual information {.smaller}

::: {.incremental}
- Measures how much information about one image is gained by knowing the other
- A perfect match has a high MI; smaller numbers are worse
- Works even when the two images have very different brightness/contrast scales
:::

![](img/registration_inputs_mi_sweep.png){.nostretch .fragment .absolute bottom="2.5%" right="12.5%" width="75%"}
![](img/registration_loss_mutual_information_sweep.gif){.nostretch .fragment .absolute bottom="2.5%" right="12.5%" width="75%"}

## Comparing the three {.smaller}

![](img/registration_loss_mutual_information.png){.nostretch .absolute bottom="10%" right="12.5%" width="75%"}


## Point-based distance {.smaller}

::: {.incremental}
- Measures the distance between corresponding landmarks in the two images
- Negated for the same reason MSE was — a perfect match scores 0, and
  every landmark that misses pulls the score down
- Simple, interpretable, with easy units (µm, pixels)
- Only measures the alignment at the landmarks themselves, not in between
:::

## Cheat sheet: which metric to use {.smaller}

::: {.fragment .absolute top="30%" left="30%"}
<table class="caption-top">
<thead>
<tr class="header">
<th>Your situation</th>
<th>Reach for</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr class="odd fragment">
<td>Same stain / same modality</td>
<td><strong>-MSE</strong> or <strong>cross-correlation</strong></td>
</tr>
<tr class="even fragment">
<td>Different stains / different modalities</td>
<td><strong>Mutual information</strong></td>
</tr>
<tr class="odd fragment">
<td>Sparse identifiable landmarks</td>
<td><strong>Point-based distance</strong></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
:::


# Similarity metric optimisation
Nudging the transformation to raise the score

## Iterative optimisation {.smaller}

::: {.incremental}
The general loop for iterative optimisation is

1. Try a transformation
2. Measure the score
3. Nudge the transformation to raise the score
4. Back to one until it stops improving
:::

![](img/registration_inputs_iterative.png){.nostretch .fragment .absolute bottom="2%" right="20%" width="60%"}
![](img/register-affine.gif){.nostretch .fragment .absolute bottom="2%" right="20%" width="60%"}

## Getting stuck: local optima {.smaller}

::: {.incremental}
- The optimiser only feels the slope directly beneath it
- So it settles on the first hilltop it reaches — not necessarily the highest
- The result can look plausible while being aligned to the wrong structure
- Written as a loss instead of a score, the same trap is called a *local minimum*
:::

::: {.fragment}
What leaves you on the wrong hilltop
:::

::: {.incremental}
- Poor starting position (images begin far apart)
- Repetitive structure — regular tissue patterns, grid-like cell arrays, tiled acquisitions
- Can be mitigated by starting coarse and refining
:::

## Local optima {.smaller}

![](img/registration_local_minima.png){.nostretch .absolute top="18%" left="18%" height="76%"}

## Phase correlation {.smaller}

For pure **translation**, we can compute the correlation between two images for
**every possible shift at once** using the **Fast Fourier Transform** — usually
called **phase correlation**.

![](img/registration_phase_correlation_1d.png){.fragment .nostretch .absolute top="45%" left="2.5%" width="95%"}

## Phase correlation {.smaller}

::: {.incremental}
1. Transform both images into **frequency space**
2. Combine them with a simple multiplication which gives a normalised correlation in frequency space
3. Transform back
4. The location of the peak directly tells you the best-aligning shift
:::

## Phase correlation {.smaller}

::: {.incremental}
- No starting guess, no iteration, no local optima — the answer is read off the peak
- Fast, and the same cost whatever the shift turns out to be
- Only works for pure translation
  - Rotation, scaling, or warping still needs the iterative route
- A good way to get a coarse starting position for that iterative route
:::

![](img/registration_inputs_phase_correlation.png){.nostretch .fragment .absolute bottom="5%" left="2.5%" width="95%"}
![](img/registration_phase_correlation.png){.nostretch .fragment .absolute bottom="5%" left="2.5%" width="95%"}



# Over- and Under-Fitting in Registration
Too much of a good thing

## Over- and under-fitting {.smaller}

::: {.incremental}
- The same trade-off as fitting a curve to noisy measurements
  - A straight line through curved data misses the real trend — **underfitting**
  - A high-order polynomial through every point chases the noise — **overfitting**
- Registration has both failure modes, in two (or three) dimensions
- The "model complexity" knob is the **transformation type**
:::

![](img/registration_fitting_compared.png){.nostretch .fragment .absolute bottom="2.5%" left="2.5%" width="95%"}

## Underfitting: too many constraints {.smaller}

::: {.incremental}
- The transformation is too simple to express the real difference between the images
- **Example:** rigid registration of sections that were genuinely stretched and
  torn unevenly during processing
- **Symptom:** structured misalignment in part of the image, and optimising
  harder doesn't help — the transform cannot express the deformation you need
:::

![](img/underfit-rigid-on-affine.gif){.nostretch .fragment .absolute bottom="2.5%" right="12.5%" width="75%"}

## Underfitting: too many constraints {.smaller}

A non-linear warp, fitted with an affine transform — the global stretch comes
out, the local warping cannot, and the score flattens out well below zero.

![](img/underfit-affine-on-nonlinear.gif){.nostretch .absolute bottom="2.5%" right="12.5%" width="75%"}

## Overfitting: too few constraints {.smaller}

::: {.incremental}
- So many degrees of freedom that any two images can be forced to match
  - A dense B-spline grid with more control points than the texture can constrain
- The score looks excellent, but the tissue is folded, implausibly
  stretched, or matched to structures that shouldn't correspond at all
:::

## Overfitting: too few constraints {.smaller}

![](img/registration_overfitting.png){.nostretch .absolute top="30%" left="2%" width="96%"}


## Finding the right level {.smaller}

The right amount of flexibility depends on how much true deformation you expect,
and how much data — landmarks, texture — you have to constrain it.

::: {.incremental}
- Start coarse and refine — rigid -> affine -> non-linear
- Adjust the regularisation terms
  - Each non-linear method has a way to penalise implausible warps
- Use a pyramid / multi-resolution approach
:::

# `brainreg`

## `brainreg` {.smaller}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="58%"}
::: {.incremental}
- Pixel-based — no landmarks to pick
- Mutual information — sample and atlas are different modalities
- Affine first, then non-linear (B-spline) — coarse to fine
- Solves on downsampled data, then applies the result to the full-resolution
  channels
:::
:::
:::

![](img/brainreg_simple.png){.nostretch .absolute right="2.5%" top="12%" height="82%"}

## `brainreg`: the essentials {.smaller}

::: {.incremental}
- **Atlas** — the target atlas
- **Data orientation** — e.g. `psl`, the position of pixel (0, 0, 0)
- **Brain geometry** — a whole brain, or a single hemisphere
- **Voxel size** — in microns, one per axis, in the same order as the data
:::

::: {.fragment}
Additional channels have no field of their own — open them as extra layers in
`napari` and they are carried through the same transformation.
:::

## `brainreg`: advanced {.smaller}

::: {.incremental}
- **Affine / freeform downsampling steps calculate** — how many levels the
  coarse-to-fine pyramid builds
  - and **… steps use** — how many of those levels it actually registers on
- **Grid spacing** — B-spline control point spacing; tighter grid, more local
  flexibility, more overfitting risk
- **Bending energy weight** — the regularisation term; how hard implausible
  warps are penalised
- **Smoothing sigma image** / **atlas** — blur before matching, so the
  optimiser sees shape rather than speckle
- **Histogram bins image** / **atlas** — how finely mutual information bins
  intensities before scoring
:::

::: {.fragment}
The defaults are tuned for whole mouse brains — reach for these when your sample
isn't one.
:::

## `brainreg`: tips {.smaller}

::: {.incremental}
- Get the orientation and voxel spacing right first
- Registration accuracy is the limiting factor, not the resolution of the atlas (typically!)
  - 25 um is usually sufficient for whole-brain registration
- **Always inspect the result**, don't just trust that it finished
  - Check the atlas boundaries against real anatomy
  - Focus on your region of interest
:::
